cover.title:
The demand is proven.
The margin is in the small print.
cover.summary: Guests already love this shop: **4.7 stars on more than 2,000 Google reviews** and 3,500+ public ratings across five sites. The menu runs on small tickets, with a **$4.00 falafel sandwich** and $3 to $5 sides. At those prices, the fixed cents on every card sale and the commission on every delivery order take a bigger share than they would at a $20 sit-down restaurant. This report shows where that happens, using only public information, and lists what to check on Olive & Za'atar's own statements.

card_fees.title: On a $4 sandwich, the 15¢ costs more than the 2.6%.
card_fees.dek: Most card fees are a percentage plus a fixed number of cents per sale. On large tickets the percentage dominates. On a menu built around $4 to $12 items, the fixed cents do, so the effective rate climbs as the ticket shrinks.

rate.note: 2.6% + 15¢ is a common published flat rate for a tapped or inserted card. It is used here as an example, not as the store's actual rate.

card_fees.rules_text: DC businesses must take cash (since Jan. 1, 2025). A card surcharge is allowed only if every fee is disclosed clearly before the guest orders. On a $4 item, a visible surcharge reads as a price increase, so lowering the cost is usually the better move than passing it on.
card_fees.unknowns_text: The real rate, the cents per sale, monthly and PCI fees, keyed-in sales, the contract end date and any equipment lease. All of it is on one monthly statement, and the franchise agreement says whether processing is the owner's choice.

delivery.title: A flat 49¢ markup can't cover a percentage commission.
delivery.dek: This store's prices on the brand ordering site vs. Uber Eats and DoorDash (both list the same prices). Taxes, fees and promotions excluded.

example_order.note: 15% to 30% is the range of the apps' standard published plans; the store's actual plan is not public.

spotlight.label: The platter gap
spotlight.note: Commission on one $44.99 Party Platter at 15% to 30%, with no markup to offset it. Catering is where a direct order is worth the most.

cards.title: Delivery closes early
cards.text: The store is open until 9:00 pm (10:00 pm Fri–Sat). On the day checked, Uber Eats and Grubhub listed delivery until 8:30 pm and DoorDash until 8:10 pm, 30 to 50 minutes before close. That may be on purpose for a small kitchen. Worth asking.

cards.title: Direct is already cheaper
cards.text: Every main costs 49¢ less at pickup, and the brand site has points. Nothing in the public journey tells a delivery guest that. "Same food, lower price, earn points" is a ready-made message for bag inserts and the counter.

fixes.title: Four fixes that cost nothing and can be done this week.
fixes.dek: None of these needs new software. They are quick wins the owner can finish this week.

items.title: Two phone numbers are live, and Apple Maps has the wrong name
items.text: The restaurant's site, Google and Yelp list **(202) 555-0142**. Grubhub and Apple Maps list **(703) 555-0199**, a Virginia number. Apple Maps also shows an old store name. iPhone and Grubhub guests may call a number that doesn't reach this store.
items.fix: claim the listing in Apple Business Connect (name and phone) and correct the Grubhub store profile. Ask who answers the 703 number today.

items.title: Delivery ends 30 to 50 minutes before the store closes
items.text: The late-evening window, when office and campus guests order dinner, has no delivery option on any app.
items.fix: check the weekend app hours too (the store is open until 10:00 pm). If the kitchen can handle it, match app hours to store hours.

items.title: Sides and the party platter carry no delivery markup
items.text: Za'atar fries, chips and hummus, and the $44.99 platter cost the same on the apps as at pickup, so the full commission comes out of margin.
items.fix: review app pricing item by item, using a percentage markup rather than a flat 49¢, within whatever the franchise allows.

items.title: The cheaper direct price is a secret
items.text: Direct pickup is cheaper and earns points, but no counter sign, bag insert or listing says so.
items.fix: a QR bag insert in every delivery order: "Order direct next time, pay less, earn points."

plan.title: Where to start: payments first, then delivery.
plan.dek: Four questions every owner asks, each answered only as far as the public evidence goes.
questions: Which systems does the franchise require: POS, ordering, loyalty, processing?
Who processes your cards today, and when does that contract end?
Roughly how many card sales a month, at what average ticket?
What share of orders comes from each delivery app, and on which commission plan?
Can you see and message the guests who earn points at your store?
research_basis: Google Maps, Yelp and Apple Maps listings
Local news coverage of the store
Truvana Tech card-fee rules by state (DC)

where_to_start.question: Switch card processor or pricing?
where_to_start.why: Small tickets: at a common 2.6% + 15¢, a $4.00 sale pays 6.35%, and 59% of that fee is the fixed cents.
where_to_start.next: read one statement for the real rate and cents per sale.

where_to_start.question: Cut delivery-app costs?
where_to_start.why: Mains carry a flat 49¢ app markup; sides and the $44.99 platter carry none, so the full commission comes out of margin.
where_to_start.next: price apps by percentage and point regulars to pickup.

where_to_start.question: Add a self-order kiosk to save labor?
where_to_start.why: Reviews praise fast service and call the shop very small. Order counts and staffing aren't public.
where_to_start.next: count peak-hour orders and staff per shift before deciding.

where_to_start.question: Get help with reviews and reputation?
where_to_start.why: 4.7★ on 2,097 Google reviews, first of 5 nearby on rating. The weak spot is listings, not reviews.
where_to_start.next: fix the phone and hours mismatches (page 6).
